It's usually the jack end. Unfortunately most newer headphones have difficult to work with enamel coated wires on them. If this is the case you have to burn off the enamel (you can use a lighter, but be prepared to lose a little wire as well), solder doesn't like to stick to it and they won't like to wrap together. You'll know these wires because they have what looks like string woven in with them.

If they have regular metal wires they will be easier to fix.

Regardless the wires are color coded, black, red, white.

Black is ground (common return)
White is left headphone.
Red is right headphone.
(Sometimes the black wire is uncoated altogether and just metal)
(There might be additional wires if you have a microphone on the headphones)

You most likely have a broken wire near the jack.

What I would do is find a jack you can cut off of something else. Cut it with a good length of wire remaining in case you screw up and need to trim it back.

Cut the jack off of your headphones back a few inches from the jack. Leave enough wire to reattach it should you decide to.

Strip about half of an inch of the insulation off of the replacement jack and headphone wires to expose the wires.

Wrap the color coded wires together being sure to keep the colors seperated.

Test it.

If it works make sure the connections are strong, then wrap them in electrical tape.

The correct method would be to solder the wires together, and use heat shrink tube to insulate them, but I am assuming that you do not have access to those tools.
